eri-silk.origin: Eri silk is produced by the eri silkworm, Samia ricini (also cited as Samia cynthia ricini or Philosamia ricini), a saturniid moth that, unlike most wild silkmoths, is domesticated and reared indoors. Its principal food plant is castor (Ricinus communis), the host implicated in its domestication; research has also examined rearing on an ancestral host, Ailanthus (Indian tree of heaven), and on cassava leaves. Production is centered in northeastern India, where the Central Silk Board's muga and eri institutes are based in Assam and Meghalaya, and eri is also reared in Thailand and elsewhere.
eri-silk.structure: Eri silk consists of fibroin filaments coated in sericin. Saturniid fibroins differ from Bombyx mori fibroin: their crystalline regions are built largely from polyalanine runs rather than the glycine-alanine repeats of mulberry silk, and eri fibroin contains the arginine-glycine-aspartic acid (RGD) cell-binding tripeptide. Comparative synchrotron FTIR, X-ray diffraction and Raman studies (Fang et al., 2016) found eri and other non-mulberry silks more extensible than mulberry silk, with properties tied to beta-sheet content, crystallinity and molecular orientation. Most cocoons are white, but some strains are red because they accumulate 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid, a tryptophan metabolite.
eri-silk.process: Larvae are fed cut castor leaves indoors. The eri cocoon is loosely built and open at one end, so its filament cannot be reeled like mulberry silk; instead cocoons, often after the moth has emerged, are degummed in soap or alkaline solutions to remove sericin, then opened and spun as a staple fiber, by hand in village production or on spun-silk machinery. Pupae are an edible by-product in parts of northeastern India, which matters for ethical claims. Eri fibroin is also hard to dissolve, which has limited its use as a regenerated biomaterial compared with mulberry fibroin.
eri-silk.performance: Spun eri yarn has a matte, cotton- or wool-like appearance and a soft, warm hand because the staple structure traps air, unlike the smooth luster of reeled mulberry silk. Its higher extensibility contributes to toughness. As a protein fiber, eri absorbs moisture, chars rather than melts, and takes acid and natural dyes, although its uptake can differ from mulberry silk. It is weakened by strong alkali, chlorine bleach and prolonged sunlight, and stored cloth can be damaged by carpet beetles and other textile pests.
eri-silk.identify: Burn tests (indicative only; use care) show silk behavior: burning with a hair-like odor and leaving a crushable ash. Saturniid silk filaments are generally flatter and wider in cross-section than Bombyx mori filaments, and FTIR or Raman spectra reflect their alanine-rich crystalline domains. Handloom eri may be confused with tussar or with spun mulberry silk waste, and blends with cotton are common, so fiber-content testing is advisable before relying on a claim of pure eri.
eri-silk.labeling: In both the US and the EU the generic fiber name is silk, and eri is a descriptive qualifier. Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011 defines silk as fiber obtained exclusively from silk-secreting insects. Terms such as peace silk or ahimsa silk, often applied to eri, are voluntary ethical claims with no legal definition; they are meaningful only if the producer documents that moths emerged before processing and states what happened to the pupae. One research group describes eri production as not sacrificing moths, but that describes a practice, not a property of the species.
eri-silk.past: Eri culture is a long-standing household activity in northeastern India, and its domestication on castor sets it apart from the wild saturniid silks. India's Central Silk Board supports eri through the Central Muga Eri Research and Training Institute in Jorhat and the Muga Eri Silkworm Seed Organization in Guwahati. Research has broadened eri rearing to castor grown on wastelands and to alternative hosts such as cassava in Thailand, and a 2026 study warned that heavy metals from contaminated sites can accumulate in edible eri pupae even when the silk itself contains little.
facts: spun staple from open cocoons, not reeled filament
mostly white; red strains accumulate 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid

tussar-silk.origin: Tussar (also tasar or tussah) is silk from several species of Antheraea, saturniid moths whose larvae feed on tree foliage rather than mulberry. In India the tropical tasar silkworm, Antheraea mylitta, feeds mainly on Terminalia arjuna, T. tomentosa and sal (Shorea robusta) and exists as regional ecoraces; its culture is a traditional livelihood for large tribal populations in Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, West Bengal and Uttar Pradesh. Temperate oak tasar, the source of Chinese tussah, comes from Antheraea pernyi, and Japan has the related Antheraea yamamai.
tussar-silk.structure: Tussar filaments are fibroin cores in a sericin coat, but they are coarser, flatter and more ribbon-like than mulberry silk. Antheraea fibroins have crystalline blocks built largely from polyalanine sequences and contain RGD tripeptide motifs, which has made A. mylitta and A. pernyi fibroins of interest as cell-adhesive biomaterials. Comparative testing reports that tasar filaments are more extensible than Bombyx mori silk, with mechanical differences linked to beta-sheet content, crystallinity and molecular orientation. The natural beige to brown color is inherent rather than dyed and varies with species, ecorace and host plant.
tussar-silk.process: Tasar rearing is largely outdoors on host trees, with larvae exposed to weather, predators and the chemistry of their host leaves; A. mylitta reared on sal performs poorly, which one study links to the high tannin and redox-active metal content of sal foliage. Cocoons intended for reeling are stifled to kill the pupae, cooked in alkaline or enzymatic solutions to soften the sericin, and reeled into raw silk, often on simple hand-operated devices. Pierced cocoons and reeling waste are degummed and hand spun into textured, slubby yarns. Woven tussar may be left in natural color or degummed, bleached and dyed.
tussar-silk.performance: Tussar is stronger and more extensible than its rustic look suggests, and its ribbon-like filaments give a textured, lower-luster surface than mulberry silk. It absorbs moisture and is comfortable in warm climates, but water can spot it and it may stiffen after washing, so gentle cleaning is usually advised. Dye uptake often differs from mulberry silk, and many fabrics are sold undyed. Like other silks it yellows and weakens with prolonged UV exposure and is damaged by alkali and chlorine bleach.
tussar-silk.identify: Burn behavior (indicative only; test with care) is that of silk. Cross-section microscopy distinguishes tussar's flat, ribbon-like filaments from the rounded-triangular profile typical of Bombyx mori, and FTIR or Raman spectra reflect the alanine-rich crystalline domains of saturniid fibroin. The trade name tussar is applied loosely, sometimes to blends or to mulberry silk finished to look similar, so species origin is best confirmed by microscopy together with supplier documentation.
tussar-silk.labeling: The generic fiber name is silk under the US Textile Fiber Products Identification Act and Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011; tussar, tasar and tussah are descriptive qualifiers for a non-mulberry type. In India, the Silk Mark scheme run under the Central Silk Board labels products verified as pure natural silk. Species, origin and blend content should be stated whenever they are claimed, because the name tussar covers several Antheraea species with different properties and geographies.
tussar-silk.past: Tasar culture developed as a forest-based activity in which communities collect or seed larvae on wild and managed host trees, which distinguishes it from the indoor, mulberry-fed sericulture of Bombyx mori. Chinese oak tussah from A. pernyi became a distinct commercial silk, and biomaterials research on its RGD-rich fibroin has grown since the 2000s. In India, tasar remains tied to tribal livelihoods across the central and eastern states, and genetic studies of A. mylitta ecoraces with microsatellite (SSR) markers document substantial diversity among regional populations, which matters for conserving seed stocks.
